answers.text: Lock the output to three fixed lines in a set order so it can't drift between runs. Each line gets a precise definition, so there's no ambiguity about what goes where.
Specify the list structure exactly: one line per call, fixed fields, a follow-up flag on each. State that the follow-up count is derived by summing the flagged entries, not asserted separately.

The timing in this note doesn't reconcile with itself. The six-hour estimate from an 8am start resolves same-day, so the note's finish date doesn't follow. It comes down to the finish date disagreeing with its own arithmetic — six hours doesn't reach the next day.
Recalculating, 96 to 118 comes out at about 23%, not the stated 20%. The on-time rate itself is consistent: 9 late out of 118 is roughly 92%, matching what's stated.

I'd sign off Output 2 — it shows the source figures and the calculation. What's missing from Output 1 is the 940 and the 827 themselves. Output 1's figure isn't necessarily wrong, only unconfirmable without an independent re-count.

I'd send Email 2 without further checking — it cites the volume figures and PO log. The claim in Email 1 that can't be checked is the rate expectation itself; nothing supports it. That doesn't make Email 1 wrong — once backed by the same volume figures, it's just as sendable.

The rate figures get redacted or held back until the tool itself is vetted. The non-disclosure clause names both parties directly, its own reason for caution beyond the rates.

The check is a fixed cross-cast — recalculate from the warehouse system, set against the drafted summary. That check sits right before the reconciliation reaches finance, not earlier in the process. Because it's a genuine cross-cast against the warehouse system, it would catch a wrong total or fabricated line.
Step 1 — extracting line items and totals — carries risk that compounds through every step after. Step 4 is where an error becomes irreversible — once it auto-submits, there's no catching it after.
